title: Manufacturing Process Selection
summary: Matching tolerance, material, quantity, and cost to the right process with capability tables and break-even analysis.

sections.heading: The Selection Problem
sections.content: Almost every part can be made several ways — machined, cast, forged, bent, molded, printed — and each route changes **cost, quality, lead time, and design freedom**. Process selection is the decision that turns a shape on a screen into a manufacturable, affordable part. The classic method: fix the **constraints first** (materials, tolerances, quantity), then pick the process that satisfies them at minimum cost — and only then design the details to suit that process.

sections.heading: Capability by Process
sections.content:
Every process has a **capability envelope** of tolerance and finish it holds economically. Typical bands:

| Process | Machining tolerance | Surface (Ra µm) |
|---|---|---|
| CNC machining | ±0.005–0.05 mm | 0.4–1.6 |
| Injection molding | ±0.1–0.5 mm | 0.8–1.6 |
| Die casting | ±0.05–0.1 mm | 1.6–6.3 |
| Investment casting | ±0.1–0.2 mm | 1.6–6.3 |
| Sheet metal | ±0.1–0.3 mm | 1.6–6.3 |
| Forging | ±0.5–1.5 mm | 3.2–12.5 |
| Sand casting | ±0.5–2 mm | 6.3–25 |
| Additive (polymer) | ±0.1–0.3 mm | 3–12 |

Read this table top-down: tighter tolerance and finish are bought with **more expensive processes**. The cheapest way to manufacture a part is almost always to relax the tolerance — so the drawing (see [[engineering-specifications|specifications]]) and the process table must be negotiated together, not sequentially.

sections.heading: Quantity Drives the Economics
sections.content:
Processes differ mainly in **tooling (fixed) vs unit (variable) cost**. The break-even quantity between two routes:

$$N_{BE} = \frac{F_2 - F_1}{u_1 - u_2}$$

with $F$ fixed tooling/setup and $u$ unit cost. Example — machining vs die casting:

| Route | Tooling F | Unit u |
|---|---|---|
| CNC machining | 2 000 | 12 |
| Die casting | 60 000 | 4 |

$$N_{BE} = \frac{60\,000 - 2\,000}{12 - 4} = 7\,250 \text{ pieces}$$

Below ~7 250 parts, machining is cheaper; above it, the die-casting tooling pays for itself. Rough quantity bands: **1–100** → machining, fabrication, additive; **100–10 000** → soft tooling, investment casting, low-volume molding; **10 000+** → die casting, injection molding, forging, progressive stamping. The crossover shifts with part complexity — the table is a starting point, the break-even formula is the truth.

sections.heading: Material–Process Compatibility
sections.content:
Materials constrain processes hard:

- **Machining**: everything machinable, but machinability varies wildly — free-cutting steels vs titanium (see [[machining-fundamentals|machining fundamentals]]).
- **Casting**: any castable alloy — grey/ductile iron, steel, aluminium, brass, zinc; not high-alloy wrought grades, and cast properties differ from wrought (lower ductility, directional solidification effects).
- **Forging**: wrought alloys shine — all structural steels, aluminium 6061/7075, titanium, nickel alloys; the flow-formed **grain alignment** is the point.
- **Injection molding**: thermoplastics only (ABS, PC, nylon, PP, POM…); thermosets and rubbers go to their own processes (compression, transfer, RIM).
- **Additive**: polymers (FDM/SLA/SLS) and metals (SLM/DED) but with **anisotropy** — printed parts are weaker across layers (see [[additive-manufacturing|additive]]).

Match the alloy to its **natural process family**: don't design a forging around a cast-only grade, and don't specify a wrought airplane alloy for a sand casting — either the process or the material must change.

sections.heading: Geometry & Feature Constraints
sections.content:
Shape features are the third hard filter (after capability and material):

- **Internal channels** — castable/moldable with cores; additive makes them free (conformal cooling!); machining needs access from outside (gun drills, EDM).
- **Undercuts** — cost tooling complexity in molding/casting (side-actions, cores) and are impossible in simple 2-axis stamping; additive ignores them.
- **Thin walls** — die casting and IM do 1–2.5 mm; sand casting needs 3–5 mm; machining needs stiffness for cutting.
- **Deep features / high aspect ratios** — forging and casting love them; machining needs tool reach (see [[cam-computer-aided-manufacturing|CAM]] for tooling constraints).
- **Axisymmetric hollow** — turning and tube forming dominate on cost; additive is the fallback for odd internal geometry.

Principle: **design the part for the least-cost process that meets function** — a bracket does not need ±0.02 mm mating faces everywhere; only the functional features do (see [[gdnt-fundamentals|GD&T]] for putting tolerance exactly where it counts).

sections.heading: The Selection Workflow
sections.content:
A repeatable order of operations:

1. **Function & tolerances** — critical dimensions from the spec sheet; separate functional from cosmetic features.
2. **Material** — from loading, environment, and cost; restrict to the process-appropriate alloy family.
3. **Quantity & forecast** — including growth; the break-even curve decides the tooling appetite.
4. **Shape screening** — internal channels, undercuts, walls, drafts: which processes are geometrically possible?
5. **Surface & finish** — Ra and appearance; cosmetic finishes may need post-processing (painting, anodizing) regardless of base process.
6. **Cost build-up** — tooling amortized over quantity: $C_{unit} = u + F/N$, plus lead time and risk.
7. **Validate with prototypes** — the chosen process's first article, before tooling commitment (see [[prototype-testing-and-validation|prototype testing]]).

Iterate: relaxing one tolerance often moves the whole part to a cheaper process family — the single highest-leverage manufacturing conversation in design.

keyTakeaways: Capability tables (tolerance + finish by process) are the first filter; relax tolerances and the process options widen immediately.
Break-even quantity N = (F2 − F1)/(u1 − u2) decides tooling investment; quantity bands are 1–100 / 100–10k / 10k+.
Match the alloy to its process family; respect geometry constraints (undercuts, walls, channels, drafts).
Run the decision workflow — function, material, quantity, shape, finish, cost — and validate with first articles.
